Suppose we do not kill ourselves off in war, or any major disaster would happen by then. What will the year 2050 will be like?
What do you think the world will be like in the year 2050?
“If you want a picture of the future, imagine a boot stamping on a human face—for ever.” ― George Orwell, 1984
Don't be so pessimistic, things are going to be fine!

Either we would be driving around in drone cars to enjoy our suddenly liberated lives since robots now do most of the labor, or we are still ridiculously and unnecessarily overworked by people who do not want the former to happen.

This is probably my favorite comment here. Either we automate everything so nobody works and have a good system to support it. Or we continue to work on things already automated to give our lives purpose.
I think the latter is more likely since most people who contribute to society get a ton of satisfaction from it.

But how many people actually work jobs that genuinely contribute something meaningful to society ( something they SHOULD be proud of ) verses people who work jobs that really don't contribute anything substantial? I'm comparing garbage men to fast food workers here ( sorry fast food workers ). Garbage men ( peoples, if you're inclined to be that PC ) are an invaluable job in our society right now, without which most of us would be dead from some fun plague or another. Fast food workers are a convenience job, pure and simple. They help grease the wheel of society without really doing anything to push it along. I'm not saying it's an easy job without merit, it's just not really contributing anything important. Now take these two people and remove their need to work these jobs to support themselves / their families. Do you think they would just sit around all day pining for their thankless jobs? I have to believe that most people would use their time bettering themselves and the world around them.

Don't confuse our own methods of tricking ourselves into believing our mundane lives have worth with the actual value of contributing something of merit to the world around us.

When I say contribute, of course it is perception. The contribution is more than the job they work, however. Anybody who makes income (in the United States) pays taxes and that could be seen as contribution, helps keep the economy going.
That being said, I don't really feel the logistics of who or who not is contributing is all that important.
While I would love to believe that the masses would flock to improve society around them, I don't believe that will happen. I believe a substantial portion certainly will, and I would like to believe I would as well in that instance, but I moreso believe the masses would flock the easy gratifications, self-satisfying acts, and otherwise things that have neutral to negative effects on society, mostly being the neutral.
If I have a week off of work, I'd want to relax and play video games and otherwise do society-neutral things. If I didn't have to work at all, I'd like to believe I'd begin more projects and do society-productive things because I would drive myself insane otherwise.
I believe society in general would always treat it like the week off of work, and grow more and more complacent and lazy.

Sorry, this turned into a really long imaginary scenario of living in the year 2050. If you don't like reading, don't bother.

I will be 65 years of age, but I won't feel like today's 65 year olds. Aside from taking good care of my body, advancements in medicine will do the rest. 65 will be today's 45.

I'll wake up in the morning, in the year 2050. I'll get dressed. Coffee and breakfast will be prepared by automated chef appliances. My shower will display the ten most relevant posts, news stories, etc. from all reaches of the Outernet (replaced the Internet in the late 20s due to government control. The Outernet uses a mesh network powered by thousands of private satellites that the government has no access to). As I brush my teeth I chuckle at a cat video. It's a shame pet ownership was made illegal by animal rights activists in the thirties.

As I get dressed I tell my house to prepare a route for my car to take me to the city. A network of computers through the house convey the information to my driverless car, programming the route to the library in city square. I look around for my Tech ID. It's essentially the combination of a wallet, cell phone, keys, etc. I ask my house to locate it for me. "Tech ID is located under papers on side table beside bed" a calm woman's voice responds. I walk into the bedroom, grab it, and head out the door.

My car is waiting for me with the conditioned air set to 70 degrees F, the ZHD monitor (768,000x432,000 pixels) bringing up my agenda for the day, and an folded up OLED display with various news on it. On the front cover of the OLED, there's a headline that yet another complex species was discovered in the Andromeda probe mission, on KELT-1b. They're creatures that can withstand unimaginable amounts of radiation from their sun. That catches my interest and I read on for a while until a soft chime interrupts my attention. It's my daughter. She's a biochemist working on the Mars VI colony. They're well on their way to the first stage of terraformation of the planet. Of course I won't be around to see the effects, but her children's children will. They're planning a vast expansion to the colony. It will be much more than a research station. They're adding housing and facilities for 500,000 people. The colony is to be named Terra Neo, as it will be a new earth in time.

Twenty minutes later, I arrive at the library. It is bustling with people. Ever since humanity found life on the fringes of our galaxy, we all shifted our focus to science and education. It was too important to fight over petty quabbles anymore. Since robotics have replaced nearly 98% of the work force, libraries and colleges have seen a major increase in visitors and attendance. We don't work anymore. Not like when I was a young adult. The government cracked down heavily on capitalist corruption toward the end of the 20s after corporate contributions were made illegal to presidential candidates. Lobbying was shut down as well. The people of the world grew tired of being pawns to their wealthy overlords and decided to take back what was theirs. Salary caps were established. Taxes on the wealthy increased. The wars stopped. Basic living wage was established. There was an abundance for everyone.

Some countries refused to join with the rest of us. Parts of nations did as well. Texas and Utah seceded from the United States. There was a bitter civil war that lasted only a couple weeks. It was over oil. Texas and Utah were forced to surrender due to the embargo of goods. Soon after, the economy crashed in those states due to the shift from fossil fuels to renewable resources. A government regulation prohibited the manufacture of internal combustion engines and other uses for petroleum and gas. That was the end to the demand for oil. Twenty years later the broken and poverty stricken states requested to join the union again. We allowed them, but it put a strain on the economy in the south. That area never recovered. Think Detroit on a state-wide scale.

I spend some time in the library, in the paper book section. Paper books have become quite rare in 2050, but there are still many of us who cherish them. While I do have a small library at home, I do love to come to the library and read what I've never read before.

For lunch I walk out onto the glass balcony that overlooks city square and take food from a cart. I don't pay, since the restructuring of the economic model has eliminated any need for that. The machines serve everyone equally.

Below me I can just barely make out the workings of the automated foundation of the city. Cargo and supplies are moved and shifted around by mechanical arms, tracks, and conveyor belts. Small drones dart in and out of alleys and streets, maintaining the machinery and keeping an eye on the workings. No one actually goes down there. There are actually entire swathes of the city that no human has entered for the last twenty or thirty years. Well, aside from manhunts when a criminal escapes into the undercity to hide out. It's quite easy to find a person down there with all of the drones.

After lunch I summon my car, which has been hovering out of sight, down toward the bottom of the tower. I get in and tell it to take the scenic route home. This route takes me around the city and up into the hills just north. Information flickers on my screen as I pass interesting buildings, large trees, and other natural features. There is a wealth of information related to anything I see. I simply need to select a feature for more information.

I arrive home, satisfied with my day. I enter the great room of my house and say "TV". A pane of glass seemingly suspended in air next to one of the walls becomes opaque and displays a few options. "Netflix". The television opens Netflix and displays the media that I can watch. "Arrested Development". A woman's voice says "I'm sorry, this television show is not available in your area. You can pay a fee of $1250 for a single use region pass if you would like to watch this feature." All we spend money on anymore is entertainment. I groan. "Yeah sure whatever." I mean it's only $1250. That's barely half of the cost of an Xbox 7k game.

I spend the next several hours vegetating in front of the TV, occasionally flipping through various social channels on my Tech ID. The evening comes to an end and I tell the house to shut all systems down.

I walk out to my balcony, pull out a cigarette, glance around to ensure no one is watching me, light it up, and take a deep drag. Cigarettes have been illegal for decades, but I have a source. I sit there, in the silence, without the usual radiation from all of my house tech, and watch the sunset. A tear falls down my cheek but I shake myself together. I think wistfully of the life of my youth. Before the machines. Before the drones. There is so much to be thankful for, yet so much that was lost.

The universe is much fuller of life in 2050, but my soul feels somewhat empty.
